I'd rather give this a neutral rating but since I have to decide I'll go with negative. I enjoy the game and will keep playing it but there are some things that just keep bothering me. The expansion may be able to address some of those but not everything can be fixed. I'd say post Title Updates Wilds has the better endgame than the base games of its modern predecessors but that wasn't exactly a high bar to begin with. Is the game worth a purchase? Honestly Rise and Sunbreak together offer all in all the better experience if you don't mind graphics and multiplayer. However if you're looking for multiplayer and your rig can handle it I'd take Wilds over World and Iceborne.

For the things that bother me:
- Graphics: it's true they patched the performance to some extend but there are things they couldn't patch like the blurriness, the fog and the brutal post processing. The game lacks visual clarity and as consequence it can be hard to tell what's going on. Their pinnacle of design is literally an all grey zone with terrible lighting where you fight a grey monster.

- floaty controls: Capcom has multiple motion cap studios and it shows. They felt like they had to animate everything but as consequence your character feels unresponsive thanks to additional intermediate animations. It's especially bad after getting hit when you're on the ground and try to get up just for some struggle animation to play. People would say old generations were clunky and had idiotic extra animations but even with things like the superman pose the controls itself were crisp and not as muddy as they are in Wilds. While it doesn't affect me frame gen will introduce additional input latency making it even worse.

- Weapons: Some are good, some are bad, at least one is so awful you could just remove it. I hated the counter focus in Rise however there you had alternatives. In Wilds they are forced upon you. I don't even get the point of 14 weapons when everything is a counter stick. A lot of people will point out that focus mode killed positioning but as someone who plays a lot solo I never need to position anyway as I'll just wait for the monster to attack me and then counter it. For me the biggest loser is the Insect Glaive even post patch as Capcom doesn't seem to know what it should be. Hammer is now "what if we turned that youtube hammer slowmotion Tigrex video into a weapon" however offsets become pretty awful once the monster have high hp and buildup resistance and outside of them at least slower weapon have a hard time dealing damage. I wouldn't even say hammer is gameplay wise bad cause I enjoy it but all the extra steps you have to do just to get the same damage as other weapons in total is frustrating. All in all if hunters weren't so absurd strong maybe monsters wouldn't require all this extra crap either.

- Seikret: They wanted a combination of Palamutes and Wirefall but made both strictly worse. Palamutes were more interactive and they weren't forced upon you. You could always bench them and use Wirebug movement as alternative. Something similar isn't possible in Wilds at all and maps are clearly designed around the Seikret. The worst is the Seikret pickup is just bad. In order to pick you up the Seikret has to physically run to you from its current random location while having collision with the monster, can be knocked over by monster attacks and will jump over ledges so the pickup will always fail at a ledge. How long this takes and in what direction the journey will go? WELL you will see. It works in the early game but once monster deal damage it can flat out cart you if you accidentally use it.

As a huge Monster Hunter fan for a long time, I understand all of the criticism coming for the game, but I want to break it down into a handful of points. So if you don't mind a moment of your time, I would love to give an extensive review on the game after many many hours, and having played the beta, and been at one of the events showcasing the game to be playable to the public before release.

1. "It's too easy"
Something I find with a lot of people when it comes to MH they play a souls-like and expect Monhun to be the same. I know this isn't everyone and I'll get into that, but first I wanna say that Monhun is a Monster Hunting game, I know shocker but that's why the game doesn't feel like some story of these over the top proportions. The lore and game is all about living with monsters and the balance of it all so applying a souls-like onto it doesn't work. On the other hand, for those who just say it's too easy, stop referencing Wilds to World, one of the biggest things in the community is saying "World is better and harder, Wilds is too easy" and truth be told, right now, it is. Because subconsciously you're relating G rank/Master rank to Low and High Rank. World had the exact same "issue" at launch for vets of the series, it's just what happens when you get good at a game comparing the skill ceiling between two games, even if in the same series is hard if you've played one before the other. I can say World is easy because I play MHG from time to time, or I could go back and play MH Tri and say it's too hard, but a Tri player could play World and say it's too easy. It's not about your skilllevel, it's about the overall level that is comfortable for casual and hardcore players. If you want a challenge, enjoy the challenge quests, or do the arch-tempered quests or fight Savage Omega.

2. Lack of Content
Jumping off of my final point on the last part, lack of content is really overstated. For all games not just Wilds. If you look at any new release now, people are BEGGING devs for content updates almost all the time. I've seen it with this community where they release a huge update and instead of enjoying it and being happy, they request more. I understand it's a large company with lots of people, but the entire company is not working on that game, a small portion of the company is working on wilds still. "well just put more people on" -you can't exactly do that when whole entire games and systems need to be made. It's a lot for a team to concept, dev, texture, everything for an update. World had just about the same time for these content updates, but now people are so pushy for things here and now to get it over with and done. This gives the game more time to breath and allow newcomers to come in and not feel overloaded, I think that's what people are forgetting.

3. Performance 
I understand the issues people are having, and I get it, but i can also say I have been able to run MH Wilds on a laptop for months now just fine. It's not a gaming laptop, it's not some custom-built model, it's a Lenovo Thinkpad. My pc which is damn near 6-8 years old and about $1000 can run wilds on high just fine with a hiccup now and then when loading zones. A game of this size, with so many well-crafted zones and thought put into every nook and cranny is bound to be powerful like this and hard to optimize. I've talked to people who want to get into game dev who have said they have no idea how Capcom has even been able to optimize so far. If you really believe games like these, of this scale aren't going to be optimization hells at launch you're mistaken. A company can't make it optimized for every single person out there because they don't know every single person's setups, so they have to try everything and see what does and doesn't work. They need player feedback, not hostile player feedback, not kind, professional feedback.

So I want to close this off by saying if you really aren't enjoying the game in its current state, take a break from it and come back. I adore this game and want to play 100s of more hours, I really do and I know I can. But I also know I want to take breaks as well to keep the spender of the game in my mind. It's such a beautiful game and not once have I felt taken out of the experience, sure when I first load in, one or two things may be polygonal, but that's also cause my GPU is old, but once it all loads in I'm right back into the immersive world that has been crafted and I've been allowed to venture into and enjoy. If you're getting tired of the difficulty of monsters, take a stroll and do some fishing or just watching the monsters and endemic life interact. That's not just a fun detail, it's apart of the game's experience, it's built for Monster Hunter. If you die and spawn at a camp, follow the palico that heals you, if you do, they run all the way back to the base camp of that area, best seen in Windward Plains. Amistrigian have an entire life cycle, Gelidron switch from oil to land to sunbathe and moisturize, the list goes on. 

Monster Hunter Wilds, and for the series in general has never been so alive than before in Wilds. It's not just about hunting the monsters or killing the boss, it's about those little moments in life that you would usually miss if you weren't looking hard enough. It's a great representation of nature and life itself, and looking past that and only staring at the flaws of the game is going to ruin the experience. I understand if its hard to see because of performance, but don't forget these are real people working on this game who have passion and love for this game just like you do. If they didn't they wouldn't be working on it in the first place. 

With that, a send off, Happy Hunting to all!

Mixed Reviews — and honestly, that’s probably a good thing.

Monster Hunter Wilds is worse than some people expected, but apparently that’s enough to declare the entire franchise a disaster. The mixed reviews are actually doing the community a favor: they help separate people who genuinely enjoy Monster Hunter from those who apparently played for five hours, got mildly inconvenienced, and immediately became professional game critics.

Is Wilds perfect? Absolutely not. It has technical issues, questionable decisions, and plenty of things that deserve criticism. But somehow, every minor flaw has been treated like Capcom personally cancelled someone’s childhood.

As an actual fan, I’d rather see honest mixed opinions than a sea of exaggerated praise. Criticism is useful when it comes from people who understand what they’re criticizing. The rest is mostly entertaining background noise.

So yes, Monster Hunter Wilds is not the masterpiece everyone wanted. It might even be worse than previous entries in some ways. And that’s okay. We can criticize it, enjoy it, discuss it, and still play the damn game.

Some people just need to remember that a game can be flawed without becoming a personal tragedy.

review:
I cannot recommend this game to anyone because the idea of rewarding Capcom with another seventy dollars for this product makes me feel physically ill. My stomach genuinely turns when I think about how much fun this series was when it wasn't awful live service slop with the gameplay loop and the weapon movesets and the monster movesets and the progression dumbed down to the point of putting you to sleep. You can spend 90 hours in a second or third generation Monster Hunter game without beating the game and you can feel like you're progressing at a completely fine speed. The only reason that this game takes 20 hours to beat is that for 17 of them you are trapped in utterly excruciating unskippable cutscenes.

Turning Monster Hunter into live service slop was bad enough, but Capcom has interpreted the existence and widespread acceptance of Title Updates into an excuse to release blatantly unfinished and untested games. The performance was bad on launch, and Capcom promised that it would fix the performance, and then it said "we will finish fixing the game in December," and now it is December and the performance is not fixed, and now it has said that the performance will be fixed in February. A year after release. A YEAR. And I just don't believe Capcom. If you do, that's wonderful wishful thinking on your part, and it brings me some happiness that you haven't got a pit of emptiness where your hope for this series once was, and that some light yet exists.

But even if the performance is fixed, too much is wrong with the game besides that. My favorite weapon, the charge blade, has been completely ruined by its moveset changes. The weapon designed to function in a switching capacity that was once considered to be the most complex weapon asks you to press the circle button and nothing else. Focus mode, in conjunction with more consistent invincibility frames, mean that positioning your character is not nearly as important as timing dodges. This was once the case only in a select few fights, and now it is the case in nearly all of them- at least, it would be, if the monsters in this game spent less time lying on the ground incapacitated and more time actually fighting you. Which they cannot. They are entirely too weak in comparison to the garbage the player is allowed to do. The retroactive adding of more 9-star monsters did not matter: their movesets were unchanged and they are still incapable of actually hitting a player who is not drooling all over his keyboard or who can't see the screen because the helmet his doctor told him he has to wear keeps slipping in front of his eyes.

I think I am only writing this review now because I heard the quest completion theme from an actually good video game when I beat the (added nine months later) final boss in what was an extremely transparent attempt to "recapture the magic" or "inspire nostalgia" that fell completely flat, having been at the end of an extremely scripted and therefore extremely uninteresting quest that was completed by mandatory NPCs who do the whole thing for you. I couldn't decide what was sadder- the thought that the developers were deliberately trying to nostalgia-bait me, or the thought that even the developers are disappointed in this game (and interviews with them give me that impression) and that it was their attempt to try to remind themselves of what great things they did in the past.

I am probably going to keep playing this game on occasion, but with nothing close to the regularity that I shall play the other actually good Monster Hunter games. There is a genuine fear in my heart that I will FOMO myself into buying the expansion, which will almost certainly be 60 USD, even though I know that the game will not be fixed by it. Wilds cannot be fixed- it is a symptom of a deeper disease: complacency- both the consumer's complacency with bad business practices and the developers' complacency with their own bad work.

[h1] The Sad End Of An Era [/h1]

I never thought I would be writing a negative review for a Monster Hunter game seeing as it was and still kind of is one of my favorite video game franchises, but here we are. In my opinion, Capcom has completely and utterly dropped the ball on this game and ruined what was once an incredibly compelling and deep gaming experience. In this review, I will illustrate my thoughts on what went wrong and why this game should be avoided for the time being.

[h2] The Gameplay [/h2]

Since the release of [i]Monster Hunter: World[/i] there has been a slow shift to make the series more accessible to newcomers with the introduction of streamlined mechanics. As someone who started with World and went back to play older games, I can say that most of these changes were welcome additions, moving the series forward from its slow and sometimes clunky roots. Wilds tries to continue this trend, but I feel as though it streamlined some mechanics too far, trivializing the experience. 

Take the new Seikret for example; what should be a fun tool that makes map traversal easier is immediately ruined when you realize that this creature knows where the monster is on the map at all times and is able to automatically take you to its location with very little input from the player. At that point, it really doesn't feel like you are hunting the monster anymore and it gives the player very little incentive to explore the map or study monster behavior which used to be a core mechanic of older games that was beloved by fans.

Another drastic change that’s been made was the decision to split defensive and offensive skills between armor and weapons respectively. I am really not sure what Capcom hoped to accomplish with this choice, because all it really did was make builds way more rigid and took away a lot of freedom when it comes to armor skills. This has resulted in an endgame build that basically fits every weapon with not a lot of deviation which feels very boring.

Speaking of endgame, that is another thing that Capcom has completely neutered. I’m not going to beat around the bush here and say that this game was unfinished at launch. [i]Monster Hunter[/i] has always been a series praised for its deep and complex endgame grind, but there has been a concerning trend that started with Rise where they release the game with only a couple of monsters to hunt for end game gear, and slowly add more monsters with content updates. This trend has continued with Wilds where, at launch, this game had 2 endgame monsters to grind. There is also the aspect of the special weapons that players are able to make from grinding these endgame monsters, which are also incredibly flawed. Basically, you get these weapon pieces from high powered endgame monsters and can build weapons out of them. You can then “reinforce” them which is basically rolling augments for more buffs. Here’s the thing though: if you don’t get the right stats for these weapons, you have to [i]Disassemble[/i] the weapon, losing those parts that you worked hard to grind for. That is an insanely unsatisfying and unrewarding system that is basically just straight up gambling for the right augments. I know the Monster Hunter series is known for its RNG-based systems, but this is getting ridiculous at this point.

[h2] The Story [/h2]

[i]Monster Hunter[/i] has never been a series known for its riveting plot lines or deep character arcs but over time it seems that Capcom has been wanting to remedy this. In World we got fully animated and voice acted cutscenes which deepend our connections to the world and characters. Then there was Rise which gave all of the NPC characters names rather than just their job title which I thought was nice. But then we come to Wilds, where the team seemingly decided to put even more emphasis on the story while simultaneously not putting any effort into making these characters memorable or have any sort of character arcs. This is the first time where I would say that the story of a Monster Hunter game actively got in the way and hindered my enjoyment. First of all, the story overall felt very rushed. You are moving from one locale to another at a breakneck pace with barely any time to get familiarized with the towns and locals. But at the same time, your crew of NPC friends that you’re on this journey with are constantly gathering with you for mandatory “yap sessions” where you all stand in a circle and talk about what has already happened in the story so far. It is so beyond frustrating because I want to take my time and get to know the locations and monsters of the area, but it feels like the game is shaking me by the shoulders and yelling at me to just get on with it. The story is basically the same as every other entry in the series, but I really feel like the developers are trying too hard to make me care about these plot points and characters when that was never really why I played these games to begin with. It makes the whole experience feel like it was born out of corporate greed rather than passion.

[h2] The Performance [/h2]

I will include my PC specs in this review to show that I’m not working with the best or worst hardware here but also to illustrate that the PC launch of this game was [i]rough.[/i] From day one, I have experienced several stability issues that have made playing this game quite frustrating to play. Frequent crashes, long load times, and graphical bugs have made me dread booting up this game because it just becomes a production. Not to mention it has that classic modern gaming touch of having to preload shaders before it can actually start. This is super frustrating, especially if I haven’t touched the game in a while because it will now take 20-30 minutes to actually load into this game. I don’t know if the RE engine is just bad when it comes to PC gaming, but so many important aspects of this game's performance just don’t work. review: I really enjoy this game more than Monster Hunter Worlds. Not having enough monsters to fight is its only problem.

Overall, an underwhelming entry to the series. 

First off, why on earth is there no option for the audio language to be classic Wyverian anymore?!
The hell do you mean, "we wanted to make people pay more attention to the dialogue." ?!

While the changes made to the weapons move sets are overall welcome and extremely refreshing, amping the tempo and dynamic ways of engaging your target, it doesn't take long to notice the cracks in the game's overall structure. 

The game has been simplified. Now, don't take this as a "this is an insult to my intellectual capability!" type of complaint. I'm a simpleton at heart, but even I think some of the simplifications in this game's gameplay loop feel just dull and unnecessary. 

The story, unsurprisingly, isn't the main reason for people to buy into this thing.
But if you make it feel like an overgloryfied tutorial, that neither respects your will to learn from experience nor your time, it will just become a massive eye roller after another, and even a reason for people, not to buy it.

While the online play was serviceable at best, it got the job done. 
In Monster Hunter World, that is. 

Many were hoping for a more seamless online experience, with friends and strangers alike.
You know... for the next game to improve on the predecessor's shortcomings and make the already good stuff even more enjoyable.

Instead, they just cramped the round based matchmaking of World into the now more open world oriented gameplay of Wilds.

How there isn't a persistent party system yet, I don't know.

The only noticeable attempt at changing the structure was the dynamic hunt mechanic, allowing you to join another player in your lobby, should he engage a roaming monster in combat.

As for the story... yes, you still have to start the mission alone and have to wait for the contained cutscene to be over, so you can invite your friends or even allow strangers to drop in.  

The roster of monsters is solid, but still sort of underwhelming.
While it's great to see some older monsters return, the overall selection of monsters seems to be suffering from the usual live service mentality of modern triple-a companies.

And paying full price, just to wait a year or two  for a multi-billion company to hand me a bunch of new monsters, which should've already been part of the "newer, bigger and better" set of promises they lured my money out the wallet with in the first place.

The only nail, missing in this coffin, would be another Iceborne move.

And don't even get me started on the horrendous technical performance.
Even after all this time, you're still required to buy expensive, top of the line hardware just to run this game.
And the sad part? It doesn't even look wort the money you spend to run it.

I wish this was taken like one or two more years trough development, instead of being released as a half-hearted excuse for a so called tripple-a title, being a live service game in disguise.

I really hope they'll finally pull their head out of their ass and fix this mess, to bring people the well deserved polish and excitement, they expected from this full priced title in the first place.

It feels like an upgraded version of World where almost all the monsters feel unique and fun to hunt. The maps are really immersive, and it’s a big jump compared to World/Rise.

But… even though all that is true, the game also has some downsides. At least for me (LS main), the game still feels clunky in a way, similar to how World did. The combos are boring and it often feels like you’re just spamming the same attack over and over. Also, the autopilot of the Seikret can ruin the exploration since it's a no-brainer mechanic. It’s a shame that, with such complex and well-designed maps, they ruin it like that.

It doesn’t have the same level of dynamism that Rise has to offer with LS, where you have a lot of combos to do, skills to choose from, and more entertaining gameplay overall. Of course, this applies mainly to LS and maybe some other weapons (I don’t know, since I haven’t played any others), but it could be the opposite for some players.

I have a friend who mains DBs, and he tells me the opposite: in Rise he spams the same attack, while in Wilds he does crazy combos and the gameplay feels much more dynamic. I know Capcom can’t make everyone happy or make all 14 weapons perfect, but I hope this gets improved in a DLC.

Other than that, the fights are pretty good and enjoyable. Maybe there are some monsters that spam attacks that one-shot you, but that’s just bad design and it only happens in the endgame. About 95% of the fights are really good.

Overall, I recommend this game to both new players and veterans. It will only get better over time with updates and DLC, and it has the potential to become the best MH ever.
